extracted.intended_audience: small business owners, policymakers, and agency staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for small entities and stakeholders on participating in Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) rulemaking — from preparing/understanding Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analyses, submitting public comments and participating in roundtables, through Final Regulatory Flexibility Analyses and potential judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRFA is the initial analysis that should describe how a proposed rule would affect small entities and consider alternatives to reduce burden. It begins the RFA process (IRFA » Public Comment » FRFA » Final Rule » Judicial Review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Comment (opportunity to respond to NPRM)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an agency issues a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) it solicits public comment; small businesses should use this opportunity to provide feedback, participate in roundtables, or otherwise engage so their concerns are considered in the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Public Feedback in Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA)
rubrics_metrics.description: FRFA weighs feedback, justifies final choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the comment period, agencies prepare a Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis that addresses the comments received, explains how feedback was considered, and justifies the agency's final decisions and chosen regulatory approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Rule requirements and inclusion of FRFA
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency, after considering public comments on a proposed rule (NPRM), establishes the final regulatory language, including any necessary revisions and their effective date. It also includes a final regulatory flexibility analysis (FRFA) if an initial analysis was required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rules must reflect consideration of the NPRM comments and, where an IRFA was required, include a FRFA explaining the agency's conclusions and any changes made in response to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Review / SBREFA enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Small businesses can sue under SBREFA for noncompliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If agencies fail to comply with RFA/SBREFA procedures (for example, by not preparing required analyses or failing to consider impacts), affected small entities have the option of judicial review to challenge the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Office of Advocacy in challenging rules and providing assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: You can challenge regulations through the Office of Advocacy by providing feedback, participating in roundtables, and utilizing the Red Tape Hotline. The Office of Advocacy also assists with regulatory flexibility analysis and can help small businesses challenge rules through judicial review if they are significantly impacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small businesses should engage with the Office of Advocacy for assistance drafting comments, participating in outreach (roundtables), using the Red Tape Hotline for problems, obtaining help with regulatory flexibility analyses, and exploring legal challenge options when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA purpose: minimize burden and avoid one-size-fits-all rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) aims to minimize the regulatory burden placed on small businesses by federal agencies and prevent 'one-size-fits-all' rules from overwhelming small enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and commenters should recognize that small firms can be disproportionately affected by regulation; analyses and comments should focus on identifying disproportionate impacts and proposing less burdensome alternatives in line with the RFA and Executive Order 13272.
